facts.claim: 作者主张圣诞晚餐什么都能省，唯独不能省拉炮里的笑话。
facts.quote: Any other component of the meal can be removed and it’s still a Christmas dinner, but take away cracker jokes and you’ve just got some people eating food.

facts.claim: 作者演示一条标准拉炮笑话的演法：先卖关子，再抛出 Elf and safety。
facts.quote: ‘Why did Santa have to wear a helmet in his workshop?’ you deliver with all the gravitas you can muster. ‘Elf and safety.’

facts.claim: 作者交代起源：早期拉炮里装的是浪漫诗，不是笑话。
facts.quote: In the early days of Christmas crackers, they contained romantic poetry rather than jokes.

facts.claim: 作者给出转折年代：一战后笑话才开始出现。
facts.quote: It was only in the years following the First World War that jokes began showing up.

facts.claim: 作者归纳拉炮笑话的三条标准：语言简单、文字游戏基础、不晦涩。
facts.quote: That means simple language, basic wordplay and nothing too intellectual or esoteric.

facts.claim: 作者以 1960 年代“来一段”的派对文化作对照：那时人人都有拿手的歌或段子。
facts.quote: as recently as the 1960s, when most entertainment was still fairly rubbish, people would often have a song they knew they could make a decent go of, or a gag they knew would do well

facts.claim: 作者给害怕上台的人一个出口：演砸了就怪拉炮厂商，且戴纸皇冠的人没资格笑你。
facts.quote: And if it goes terribly, you have an escape clause (the second-best festive Claus)

relations.relation: 载体更换的原因是娱乐方式变多：有了唱片机，没人愿意听一桌人念蹩脚诗，笑话更快也更大众。
relations.quote: once you had a record player, you weren’t going to sit through a table’s worth of people reciting dreadful poetry.

relations.pair: 家庭场合 / 多代可懂
relations.relation: 圣诞是家庭场合，所以笑话必须跨代可懂；作者用“前任装饰品”这种需要背景知识的梗作反例。
relations.quote: Christmas is a family occasion, so a good cracker joke needs to be understood by multiple generations of people.

relations.relation: 1960 年代的派对表演文化早于“社交尴尬”与 cringe 这类概念，作者以此解释今天为什么没人敢演。
relations.quote: This was long before concepts like social awkwardness or ‘cringe’

relations.relation: 结尾用 escape clause 与 Claus 的谐音收束，再用 elf-esteem 叠一层圣诞双关。
relations.quote: why is it nice to make people feel good about themselves at Christmas? To boost their elf-esteem.

numbers.meaning: 笑话进入拉炮的时间分界：一战之后。
numbers.quote: It was only in the years following the First World War

numbers.meaning: 作者把“人人表演一段”的黄金期定在晚至 1960 年代。
numbers.quote: as recently as the 1960s, when most entertainment was still fairly rubbish

numbers.meaning: 百年前拉炮里的早期笑话，有些今天仍成立。
numbers.quote: some of the earliest ones found in century-old crackers would just about work today

numbers.meaning: 作者主张每年至少练一次当众表演的胆量。
numbers.quote: there’s surely something to be said for stretching your public-performance bones once a year
